name: Aaron Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play junior keyboard parts for a theatre, edit cue recordings and teach six children on Saturdays. I finished secondary school and still ask the sound lead to check difficult parts; the show is a good place to learn when everyone gets paid.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mira works in a school kitchen, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The theatre pays well for this job, we have about nine months of expenses saved, and other theatres are close enough to audition for.

I'd keep **in-person lessons** because beginners need someone beside the instrument.
think: Our **nine-month reserve** and signed theatre season keep the mortgage secure.
Occasional **AI use** helps with lists but is not part of my pay plan.
do: Keep **Tuesday rehearsals** and six Saturday pupils through the signed season.
Fund **equipment repairs** from paid cue fees only after wages, travel and family bills clear.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and household bills this year.
S0.quote: A quick rehearsal list will not catch the keyboard entrance I miss.
fieldNote: His **signed season** and nine-month reserve protect the mortgage from a delayed cue fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre crew a quicker rehearsal list is fine, but a missed keyboard entrance is still mine to fix. The Saturday pupils also need me to show them the notes in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI sometimes to tidy a set list after our sound lead shows me a tool, but the pay plan is not built on it. We have about nine months of expenses saved and a signed theatre season, so a small change leaves the mortgage safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the Tuesday theatre rehearsals and six Saturday keyboard pupils through the signed season. I'll put part of each paid cue-editing fee into the equipment repair envelope only after wages, travel and family bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because the season and teaching fees cover the next year. I can deal with a delayed cue edit without touching the house reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened the last time a matinee moved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A producer moved one matinee last year. The theatre still paid for rehearsals, and the pupils covered the week until the show returned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks a new schedule with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check a new schedule with the players before promising a family weekend away. Our two children have heard enough last-minute theatre changes to ask whether the dates are signed. A quick rehearsal list will not catch the keyboard entrance I miss.

I'd keep **live cue checks** even if software drafts the sheet.
think: **Cue edits and demos** make a quarter of my pay and could shrink.

do: Compare **paid cue hours** with the theatre's new contract this month.
Test **proven AI** on owned audio after licence checks; compare every instrument with the original and keep trials off shared drives.
Seek a **posted paid assistant slot** only if the theatre refuses two paid rehearsals.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing a quarter of my pay.
S1.quote: The mortgage needs regular money, not a cleverer cue sheet.
fieldNote: His **quarter-income exposure** lies in editing rather than the physical keyboard part of the show.
His **tool trial** requires demonstration, licence, owned audio and a stop rule for missing cues.

steps.text: Compare paid cue hours with proposed theatre contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the producer that software may make cue sheets quickly, but paid rehearsal is still how the show holds together. I would ask for the keyboard player's rehearsal hours to remain in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cue editing and simple demo work make about a quarter of my pay, and I expect those fees to shrink. Nine months saved gives us time to adjust. The mortgage needs regular money, not a cleverer cue sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare last season's paid cue hours with the proposed contract. In the first year of change, I'll test an AI stem-separation tool, which splits recordings into separate parts, on my own rehearsal file only after our sound lead demonstrates it, the licence permits it and I can check every instrument against the original.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing those paid hours, even with savings. I am still learning the keyboard parts, so I cannot simply replace a quarter of my fee with better solos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop a faulty audio tool affecting the show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the file off the theatre's shared drive until the trial is clean. If it drops a singer's entrance, I would stop and go back to the original recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What paid rehearsal minimum would you request?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the producer for two paid keyboard rehearsals before each opening. If the theatre refuses, I would ask one of the nearby venues about a posted paid assistant slot, not quit over a rumour.

I'd keep **paid shows** while human players are still booked.
think: **AGI in 2028** could remove cue fees before robots play around 2031.

do: Get next season's **dates** and total paid cue fees this week.

feel: I feel **anxious** about losing cue pay, with savings to search.
S2.quote: An audition is a chance, but a signed paid season is a wage.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 editing loss** from the 2031 robot threat to playing.
His **job switch** requires a posted role, qualifying test, childcare-compatible hours and a written net offer.

steps.text: Get next season's written paid rehearsal dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the producer that AGI in 2028 could write every cue sheet we sell, so we need the paid hours spelled out now. I would keep turning up for shows while the theatre signs them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028, full AGI could edit cues, draft lessons and arrange demos for less than I earn. Robots able to handle keyboard parts arrive around 2031, but my thinking-work fees could fall first; our reserve and many local theatres let me search without missing the mortgage next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll get next season's rehearsal dates in writing and total my cue fees. In the first year after 2028, if cue work halves, I'll apply for a posted keyboard assistant job at another theatre only if my playing test qualifies and written net pay after travel replaces the lost fee; I'll keep my pupils meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about an expected loss in cue pay. I can afford an audition, but I still need another theatre to offer real hours before changing jobs. An audition is a chance, but a signed paid season is a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a keyboard assistant opening posted now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A nearby theatre held auditions last year, but none is posted now. I would phone about its requirements before using a school day for an audition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would a new shift fit school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira works in a school kitchen and can cover pickup only on Thursdays. I would reject an offer that needs me at the theatre when both children are leaving school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre five years gives us time to train people to run a room, not just press a key. I would ask for a paid trainee shift for stage sound if the budget can bear it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 might take cue editing and lesson plans; robots able to run hands-on stage work arrive around 2034. Ordinary software may cut my editing fees earlier, so I need a skill that pays while the theatre still hires people to set up shows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the technical college about a live-sound certificate if its grant covers fees and two nearby theatres accept it. I'll enrol only if Mira's kitchen rota covers the children's evenings; in the first year after 2031, I'll seek paid sound shifts only if I qualify and a theatre posts them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because the editing pay may fade before the course is finished. A grant makes the course possible, but it does not guarantee a theatre needs another junior technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy equipment to start training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college has practice consoles, so I would not buy one. If the class clashes with Mira's late night, I will take the next intake instead of paying a sitter from our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check that a theatre needs trainees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the producer what paid sound shifts they expect next season before enrolling. A trainee title without a rate is not a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the theatre a decade is enough to build a teaching room and a dependable live audience. I would still show pupils the new tools after a trusted player has proved what they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, I will need paid work; robot players around 2039 may reach the pit. Cue fees may fall well before 2036, so I want school teaching and a small live series with signed terms, not a plan that depends on my current theatre forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the community hall for a monthly beginner keyboard session only if six families prepay, the hall confirms its low room fee and another adult can supervise the children. By 2036 I'll keep at least nine months saved from signed teaching and theatre fees; in the first year after AGI, I'll continue the session only if six families renew and net fees still cover room and my teaching time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because cue work can thin out long before the ten years end. The reserve keeps the mortgage safe for a while, but a class needs paying families each term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must the hall confirm before you announce a class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall manager has shown me the room, but the evening price is still unsettled. The second adult would need to be named before a child arrives. A room offered by word of mouth is not a paid class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop the existing pupils for a school post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would also keep my Saturday pupils until a school offers real paid hours. I don't have a school post in hand, and I won't move the children's schedule for a rumour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because cue editing fees could fall before I have sound qualifications or another paid theatre offer. Written rehearsal dates, posted jobs and a course the local theatres accept would let us make a move without risking the mortgage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who checks the singer's entrance after a tool separates the tracks. The player on stage still has to hear the breath before the cue.

headlineQuote: The player on stage still has to hear the breath before the cue.
portrait: Aaron is a **43-year-old** junior keyboard player with secondary schooling, theatre work, cue editing and six young pupils.
He and Mira have **two children**, a mortgage, high junior pay and about nine months saved, with nearby theatres.
He uses **AI occasionally** after trusted demonstration and expects cue fees to shrink before robots reach stage work.
He tests **sound training** and paid classes only with accepted credentials, childcare, signed room terms and confirmed fees.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because cue editing fees could fall before another paid theatre role is offered.
whatWouldHelp: **Written theatre dates**, real vacancies and accepted sound training would help him replace lost fees safely.
